entries.meaning: The workhorse of the English relative system, and the only relative that is at home with both people and things. It marks off the clause that tells you which one.
examples: The bill that passed last night wasn't the one anybody had read.
He's one of the few engineers that have read the original specification.
The apartment that we looked at on Tuesday is already rented.
That's the folder that I pulled the numbers from.
Everything that could go wrong on that drive did.
She's the only reporter that got the mayor on the record.
Nothing that he said afterward changed a single vote.
It was my sister that first noticed the smell of gas.

senses.head: Subject of its own clause
body: The gap is the subject; that cannot be dropped here.
examples: The bill that passed last night wasn't the one anybody had read.
He's one of the few engineers that have read the original specification.

senses.head: Object of its own clause
body: The gap is the object; here that is optional and speakers usually leave it out.
examples: The apartment that we looked at on Tuesday is already rented.
That's the folder that I pulled the numbers from.

senses.head: After superlatives, quantifiers, and indefinite pronouns
body: The frame where that beats which and who even for writers who otherwise mix them freely.
examples: Everything that could go wrong on that drive did.
She's the only reporter that got the mayor on the record.
Nothing that he said afterward changed a single vote.

senses.head: In it-clefts
body: The construction that pushes one element to the front for emphasis.
examples: It was my sister that first noticed the smell of gas.

entries.pronunciation note: the weak form is the normal form here; the strong /ðæt/ THAT shows up only when the word is being quoted or contrasted. This is the reliable way to hear the difference between relative that and the demonstrative: the car that broke down /ðət/ versus that car /ðæt/.
entries.русский: который — универсальное относительное о людях и о вещах, в ограничительных придаточных без запятых
entries.case: none — one form for subject and object; it has no genitive and can never follow a preposition
entries.register: neutral, at every level from conversation to Supreme Court opinions
entries.type: relative pronoun (some modern grammars call it a relativizer rather than a true pronoun)
entries.person / number: invariant. Third person by default; number and person are supplied by the antecedent and surface on the verb, never on that.
entries.refers to: people, animals, things, and abstractions alike — the woman that called, the dog that bit him, the report that arrived. It cannot take a whole clause as its antecedent; for that use which. It is the strongly preferred relative after superlatives (the best movie that), after all, any, every, only, no, few, much, little, after indefinite pronouns (everything that, anyone that), and in it-clefts (it was Marie that noticed).
entries.agreement: when that is the subject of its clause, the verb agrees with the antecedent: the file that is missing, the files that are missing. In one of the [plural] that, the antecedent is the plural noun, so the verb is plural — one of the few people that know the code. Only when the only is added does it go singular: the only one of the guards that was awake. When the antecedent is itself a pronoun or a quantified noun, that antecedent's own number decides, and the classes are fixed: the compound indefinites everyone, everybody, someone, somebody, anyone, no one, nobody are singular (everyone that wants a copy, somebody that knows the system, nobody that has read it), and so are each, every, either, and neither (each report that is filed, neither copy that was returned); both, several, few, and many are plural (both files that were attached, the few that remain); all, some, and most take the number of what they actually refer to (all the pages that were missing against all the gravel that was delivered); and none is the one word here that goes either way, taking a singular or a plural verb with both fully standard — none of the reports that came in was useful presses the "not one" reading, none of the reports that came in were useful is the commoner choice in edited American prose.
entries.pattern: [noun] that [verb] … — subject of its clause · [noun] that [subject] [verb] — object of its clause · [noun] that [subject] [verb] [preposition] — stranded, as in the office that I called from · never ✗ [preposition] that · never ✗ , that
entries.contrast: Against which: in edited American prose that takes the restrictive clauses and which the nonrestrictive ones, but only one direction of that rule is absolute — that is impossible in a nonrestrictive clause, while restrictive which is merely something a copy editor will change. Against who: that with a human antecedent (the man that hired me) is standard and has been since Old English; a minority of readers dislike it, so who is the safer choice when the antecedent is a named individual. Against the complementizer that (he said that he'd come): the relative fills a slot inside its clause — take it away and there is a hole (the report [that] arrived → …arrived has no subject); the complementizer fills no slot — take it away and the clause is still complete.
entries.see also: which, who, zero relative, whose, that (determiner), that which, that (complementizer), that (relative connector)

entries.meaning: The relative for things, and the everyday choice when the antecedent is a whole idea rather than a noun.
examples: Her second novel, which took nine years, sold about four hundred copies.
The engine, which had been rebuilt twice, finally seized on the interstate.
The provisions which survive termination are listed in Schedule C.
The file cabinet in which the originals were stored burned with the building.
That's the argument to which I keep coming back.
He turned down the offer, which everyone else thought was insane.
She never explained why she left, which is her right.
There were forty-two proposals, six of which missed the deadline outright.
The bylaws, which nobody had read since 1974, turned out to settle the question.

senses.head: Nonrestrictive relative
body: Commas on both sides, and the clause could be lifted out without changing what the sentence is about.
examples: Her second novel, which took nine years, sold about four hundred copies.
The engine, which had been rebuilt twice, finally seized on the interstate.

senses.head: Restrictive relative
body: No commas. Grammatical, standard in British English, common in American legal and technical writing — and routinely changed to that by American editors.
examples: The provisions which survive termination are listed in Schedule C.

senses.head: After a preposition
body: The pied-piping frame. Here that is impossible, the zero relative is impossible, and no editor objects to restrictive which.
examples: The file cabinet in which the originals were stored burned with the building.
That's the argument to which I keep coming back.

senses.head: Sentential relative
body: The antecedent is the whole preceding clause, not any noun in it. Always preceded by a comma. The trap: if the reader can find a noun that might be the antecedent, they will try it first, so keep the clause short and the reference obvious.
examples: He turned down the offer, which everyone else thought was insane.
She never explained why she left, which is her right.

senses.head: In a partitive phrase
body: With a quantifier or a number in front of it.
examples: There were forty-two proposals, six of which missed the deadline outright.

senses.head: Object of the verb in its own clause
body: The gap is the object rather than the subject, and which keeps the same form either way — it has no whom.
examples: The bylaws, which nobody had read since 1974, turned out to settle the question.

entries.pronunciation note: weak /wətʃ/. For most Americans which and witch are homophones; older speakers and many in the South and Appalachia keep the breathy /ʍɪtʃ/ that distinguishes them. The wh- here is the same Old English hw- that gives who its /h/.
entries.русский: который — относительное о вещах; в придаточных с запятыми или отсылка ко всему предложению
entries.case: none — one form for subject and object; the genitive is whose or of which
entries.register: neutral; the only option in a nonrestrictive clause about a thing, and the formal option after a preposition
entries.type: relative pronoun; also interrogative, and a determiner when it precedes a noun
entries.person / number: invariant, third person; singular or plural entirely according to the antecedent
entries.refers to: things, animals, institutions, and abstractions — never a person. ✗ the woman which called was ordinary English in 1611 (Our Father which art in heaven) and is a plain error now. Companies, teams, and committees count as things in American English (the company, which), though the band who is heard when the group is being thought of as its members. Among the ordinary relatives only which can take an entire clause as its antecedent; the one other word that does the same job is sentential as, which is confined to a narrower frame and, unlike which, may also stand in front of the clause it comments on (As everyone expected, the vote was postponed).
entries.agreement: as subject, the verb agrees with the antecedent — the box, which is heavy; the boxes, which are heavy. With a whole clause as antecedent the verb is singular: He said nothing, which was answer enough. With a collective antecedent American English takes the singular: the committee, which has met twice.
entries.pattern: [noun], which [verb] … · [noun], which [subject] [verb] … · [preposition] which [subject] [verb] — pied-piped, as in the shelf on which it sits · [quantifier] of which — three of which, all of which · [clause], which [verb] — the sentential relative
entries.contrast: Against that: see the honest version above — that is barred from nonrestrictive clauses absolutely, while restrictive which is grammatical but will be edited. Against who: things versus people, with no overlap. Against the fused relative what: which needs an antecedent sitting in the sentence, what contains its own (I heard what you said = the thing that you said).
entries.see also: that, who, whose, of which, all of which, some of which, none of which, by which, in which, on which, q.v. (quod vide) / which see, which (determiner), in which case, whichever, fused relatives

entries.meaning: The relative for people, filling the subject slot of its clause — and, in everything short of formal writing, the object slot as well.
examples: The nurse who took my blood pressure had been on shift for fourteen hours.
Anyone who still has a paper ticket should come to the front.
There's nobody in this office who knows how to reset the alarm.
My grandmother, who never learned to drive, walked everywhere until she was eighty.
It was Ruiz who filed the original complaint, not his partner.
The candidate who we all assumed would win finished third.
He's the one who I gave the spare key to.
The contractor who she hired last spring never finished the deck.

senses.head: Subject of its own clause, restrictive
body: No commas; the clause says which person.
examples: The nurse who took my blood pressure had been on shift for fourteen hours.
Anyone who still has a paper ticket should come to the front.
There's nobody in this office who knows how to reset the alarm.

senses.head: Subject of its own clause, nonrestrictive
body: Commas; the person is already identified.
examples: My grandmother, who never learned to drive, walked everywhere until she was eighty.
It was Ruiz who filed the original complaint, not his partner.

senses.head: Subject across an intervening clause
body: We thought, they said, everyone assumed — these do not change the case.
examples: The candidate who we all assumed would win finished third.

senses.head: Object of its own clause
body: Where formal writing wants whom, and where speech does not.
examples: He's the one who I gave the spare key to.
The contractor who she hired last spring never finished the deck.

entries.pronunciation note: weak /(h)ʊ/ — the vowel shortens in running speech (the man who called), but unlike him and her the /h/ normally survives. Who's /huz/ is who is or who has, and is pronounced exactly like whose.
entries.русский: который, кто — относительное о людях, обычно подлежащее своего придаточного
entries.case: subject (nominative) in the paradigm — object form whom, genitive whose — but in present-day American English who also fills the object slot everywhere except directly after a preposition: the agent who we hired, the agent who I gave it to, but never ✗ the agent to who I spoke
entries.register: neutral as a subject; as an object it is the ordinary spoken form and increasingly the written one
entries.type: relative and interrogative pronoun
entries.person / number: invariant in form; any person, either number. It transmits the person of its antecedent to the verb: I who am …, you who are …
entries.refers to: people, and animals granted personal status (our dog, who hates the mail carrier). Not things: ✗ the report who arrived. American English treats collective nouns as things and uses that or which for them (the committee that voted), though the band who turns up when the members rather than the body are meant.
entries.agreement: as subject, the verb agrees with the antecedent in number and person: the neighbor who lives upstairs, the neighbors who live upstairs, It is I who am to blame (formal). The classic trap: one of those people who do this takes the plural, because who points at those people; the only one of my friends who has a truck takes the singular, because who points at the only one. With an indefinite-pronoun antecedent the verb inside the relative clause is singular — everyone who wants a copy, somebody who knows the system, nobody who was on the call — even though the pronoun that picks that antecedent up later in the sentence is normally singular they: Everyone who wants a copy should raise their hand. Singular they is standard American English, accepted by the AP, Chicago, MLA, and APA manuals with differences only of scope (see they), and it leaves the relative clause's own verb singular. One honest footnote to It is I who am to blame: that is the formal pattern, and the reason person agreement is worth knowing at all, but the ordinary American sentence is It's me who's to blame or It's me that's to blame. It's me is standard English, not a lapse — the subject form after be is a Latin-modeled rule that American usage has left behind (see personal pronouns).
entries.pattern: [person noun] who [verb] … — subject · [person noun] who [subject] [verb] — object, standard in speech: the guy who I met · [person noun] who [subject] [verb] [preposition] — stranded: the guy who I gave it to · [person noun], who [verb] … , — nonrestrictive · never ✗ [preposition] who
entries.contrast: who vs. whom is decided by the he/him test: rebuild the relative clause as a sentence and put he or him in the gap. The agent who handled the sale → he handled the sale → who. The agent whom we hired → we hired him → whom. Do not let a parenthetical clause fool you: in the candidate who we thought would win, the gap belongs to would win (he would win), so it is who, and ✗ whom we thought would win is a hypercorrection — now a more common error than the one it was meant to prevent. who's vs. whose: expand it. If who is or who has fits, it is who's; otherwise whose. Against that: both are standard for people in restrictive clauses, but only who can appear in a nonrestrictive one. One case decision the relative does not make: a coordination sitting inside the relative clause is settled on its own by the deletion test — the clients who my partner and I signed (delete my partner and: ✗ me signed), the clients who signed with my partner and me (✗ with I). The two failures are the familiar pair, ✗ Me and him went on one side and the hypercorrections ✗ between you and I and ✗ They invited my wife and I on the other; the correct forms are between you and me and He gave it to Bob and me, and the whole subject belongs to personal pronouns.
entries.see also: whom, whose, that, zero relative, to whom, for whom, with whom, those who, whoever, who's, interrogative pronouns, personal pronoun case

entries.meaning: The object form, used where the person is on the receiving end of the verb or the preposition.
examples: The attorney to whom the case was reassigned had never tried a jury case.
The people with whom we shared the cabin turned out to be cousins of my father's.
He's the sort of man about whom nobody has a strong opinion.
The candidate whom everyone had written off won by nine points.
She wrote to the senator, whom she had met exactly once, and got an answer in a week.
Several of the workers, three of whom had been there since the plant opened, refused to sign.
He thanked the volunteers, most of whom had driven in from out of state.

senses.head: After a preposition
body: The pied-piped frame — formal, and the last stronghold of the word.
examples: The attorney to whom the case was reassigned had never tried a jury case.
The people with whom we shared the cabin turned out to be cousins of my father's.
He's the sort of man about whom nobody has a strong opinion.

senses.head: Object of its own clause
body: Formal writing; ordinary speech uses who or nothing at all.
examples: The candidate whom everyone had written off won by nine points.
She wrote to the senator, whom she had met exactly once, and got an answer in a week.

senses.head: In a partitive phrase after a quantifier
body: Nonrestrictive, always after a comma, and the frame where no substitute exists.
examples: Several of the workers, three of whom had been there since the plant opened, refused to sign.
He thanked the volunteers, most of whom had driven in from out of state.

entries.pronunciation note: weak /(h)ʊm/, and in rapid speech reduced all the way to /(h)əm/ — to whom comes out /tə əm/ and several of whom /ˈsɛvrəl ə əm/. The /h/-dropping is the ordinary unstressed-syllable process that also gives him /ɪm/, her /ɚ/, them /əm/, you /jə/, and he /i/; the full table is under weak forms.
entries.русский: которого, которому — объектная форма who; книжн., обязательна после предлога
entries.case: object
entries.register: formal in the bare relative use; neutral and unavoidable after a preposition
entries.type: relative and interrogative pronoun
entries.person / number: invariant; any person, either number; people only
entries.refers to: human antecedents only, plus animals treated as persons. Things take which: the agency to which he reported, not ✗ to whom.
entries.agreement: none of its own. As an object it never controls a verb, so the verb of the relative clause agrees with that clause's own subject: the officers whom the board has cited — has agrees with board.
entries.pattern: [person noun] [preposition] whom [subject] [verb] — pied-piped: the agent to whom I spoke · [person noun] whom [subject] [verb] — plain object: the agent whom I called · [person noun], [quantifier] of whom [verb] … — four of whom, all of whom · than whom — a fossil, as in a scholar than whom none was more careful · never ✗ that whom, never ✗ whom as a subject
entries.contrast: whom is the object form of who, and the he/him test settles every case: put he or him in the gap and see which one fits — we hired him → the agent whom we hired. Two honest observations about how much of it survives. First, outside prepositional position American English has very largely replaced it with who, and the agent who we hired is standard in speech and increasingly in print; using whom there is a register choice, not a correctness requirement. Second, immediately after a preposition whom is still obligatory in writing — ✗ to who is an error — and this is where even whom-avoiders produce it naturally. The one thing to avoid outright is the hypercorrection ✗ whom shall I say is calling, ✗ the candidate whom we thought would win: the pronoun there is the subject of the inner verb, so it must be who.
entries.see also: who, whose, which, to whom, for whom, with whom, both of whom, several of whom, many of whom, whomever, than whom, than

entries.meaning: The one relative that marks possession, and the one that does not care whether its antecedent is human.
examples: The novelist whose letters were auctioned last year had asked that they be burned.
Any student whose name appears on this list should see the registrar before Friday.
She's the one whose car got towed on Tuesday.
We finally bought a house whose roof doesn't leak.
It's an argument whose logic falls apart the moment you check the numbers.
There's a bill in committee whose effects nobody has bothered to model.
The company, whose founder resigned in March, has lost half its engineering staff.
They finally located the contractor in whose warehouse the crates had sat for a year.

senses.head: With a human antecedent
examples: The novelist whose letters were auctioned last year had asked that they be burned.
Any student whose name appears on this list should see the registrar before Friday.
She's the one whose car got towed on Tuesday.

senses.head: With an inanimate antecedent
body: Standard, and lighter than any alternative.
examples: We finally bought a house whose roof doesn't leak.
It's an argument whose logic falls apart the moment you check the numbers.
There's a bill in committee whose effects nobody has bothered to model.

senses.head: In a nonrestrictive clause
examples: The company, whose founder resigned in March, has lost half its engineering staff.

senses.head: After a preposition
body: Whose pied-pipes like which and whom, carrying both the preposition and the following noun to the front of the clause.
examples: They finally located the contractor in whose warehouse the crates had sat for a year.

entries.pronunciation note: weak /(h)ʊz/ · a perfect homophone of who's (= who is, who has), which is the whole reason the spelling gets confused
entries.русский: чей, которого — притяжательная форма относительного, о людях и о вещах
entries.case: possessive (genitive)
entries.register: neutral with human antecedents; neutral with inanimate ones in every register except the most conservative copydesk
entries.type: relative genitive — the possessive of both who and which; also interrogative. Inside its clause it behaves like a determiner, since a noun always follows it, but it is the element that links the clause, and grammars have called it a relative pronoun for four centuries
entries.person / number: invariant. The following noun controls number, not the antecedent.
entries.refers to: both people and things — a violinist whose bow arm is failing, a house whose roof leaks, a statute whose intent is obvious, a dog whose owner never showed up.
entries.agreement: the verb agrees with the noun that whose introduces, not with the antecedent: a house whose windows are boarded up (plural verb after a singular antecedent), houses whose roof is shared (singular verb after a plural one).
entries.pattern: [noun] whose [noun] [verb] … — the whose-phrase is the subject of the relative clause · [noun] whose [noun] [subject] [verb] — the whose-phrase is its object: the writer whose books I collect · [noun] [preposition] whose [noun] [subject] [verb] — pied-piped: a company in whose warehouse the crates sat for a year · [noun], whose [noun] [verb] … , — nonrestrictive
entries.contrast: whose vs. who's — expand the contraction; if who is or who has works, write who's, and if it does not, write whose. whose vs. of which for inanimate possessors — both are correct and mean the same thing, but whose is almost always the better sentence: a house whose roof leaks against the stilted a house the roof of which leaks. The rule that whose may refer only to people is a zombie rule: inanimate whose has been in continuous use since Middle English, appears in Shakespeare, Milton, and the King James Bible, and is endorsed by Fowler, Garner, and Merriam-Webster's usage dictionary alike. This entry covers the relative use; for the question word before a noun (Whose coat is this?) see the determiner file.
entries.see also: who, whom, which, of which, whose (determiner), of which (determiner), whosever, who's

entries.ipa: none — the pronoun is not pronounced because it is not there. What a listener actually hears is a bare juncture: two noun phrases butted together with no pause and no /ðət/ between them — the book I read /ðə ˈbʊk aɪ ˈrɛd/. Pausing at the gap is what makes a learner sound like they have lost their place. Written with the symbol Ø in grammars; written with nothing at all in real life.
entries.meaning: The relative pronoun you get by leaving the relative pronoun out. English has allowed it since the Middle Ages, and in conversation it is more common than that.
examples: The apartment Ø we looked at on Tuesday is already rented.
Everything Ø she owns fits in the back of one car.
The one thing Ø nobody mentioned was what it would cost.
That's the guy Ø I was telling you about.
The years Ø we spent in Tucson were the best ones we had.
He's not the man Ø he was ten years ago.
There's a woman downstairs Ø says she has an appointment.

senses.head: Object of the verb in its clause
examples: The apartment Ø we looked at on Tuesday is already rented.
Everything Ø she owns fits in the back of one car.
The one thing Ø nobody mentioned was what it would cost.

senses.head: Object of a stranded preposition
examples: That's the guy Ø I was telling you about.
The years Ø we spent in Tucson were the best ones we had.

senses.head: Complement of be
examples: He's not the man Ø he was ten years ago.

senses.head: Subject after existential there — spoken only
examples: There's a woman downstairs Ø says she has an appointment.

entries.русский: нулевое относительное — пропуск «который» в роли дополнения: the book I read
entries.case: the missing element is an object or a complement, never a subject in edited writing
entries.register: neutral to informal; ordinary in speech and in all but the most formal prose. It is not a contraction, not slang, and not an error.
entries.type: zero relative, also called the contact clause — a relative pronoun omitted rather than replaced
entries.person / number: no form, so nothing to inflect.
entries.refers to: anything that could refer to — people, things, ideas — but only in restrictive clauses. Never in a nonrestrictive one: ✗ my car, I bought in June, is already dead.
entries.agreement: none of its own. The relative clause keeps its own subject, and that subject controls the verb: the emails Ø she sent are missing.
entries.pattern: [noun] Ø [subject] [verb] — the movie we saw · [noun] Ø [subject] [verb] [preposition] — stranded, and the commonest shape of all: the guy I told you about · [noun] Ø [subject] [verb] [complement] — the man he was · never ✗ [noun] Ø [verb] in edited writing · never ✗ [preposition] Ø
entries.contrast: Against that: fully interchangeable whenever the relative is an object — the book that I read and the book I read differ only in weight. The test for whether you may drop it is mechanical: look at what comes right after the gap. Another subject? Drop it. A verb? Keep it. The file [that] I sent — I follows, so it goes. The file that arrived — a verb follows, so ✗ the file arrived was corrupt is broken English. It also cannot be dropped from a nonrestrictive clause, and there is nothing to drop when the preposition has been pied-piped (the man to whom I spoke). One recognized exception runs the other way: after existential there and in clefts, spoken American English does drop a subject relative — There's a man Ø wants to see you, It was my brother Ø told me — which is widespread, old, and still changed by every copy editor.
entries.see also: that, which, whom, who, zero that

entries.term: all of which, some of which, none of which
entries.ipa: /ˌɔl əv ˈwɪtʃ/, /ˌsʌm əv ˈwɪtʃ/, /ˌnʌn əv ˈwɪtʃ/
entries.meaning: A quantifier and a relative pronoun joined by of, letting a second clause comment on part of what the first clause introduced.
examples: She left behind eleven boxes of papers, most of which had never been opened.
The bill adds four new fees, none of which was mentioned in the summary. (were is equally standard here)
He gave three reasons for the delay, all of which turned out to be false.
The house came with two furnaces, neither of which was under warranty.
They tested sixty samples, some of which had been sitting in a garage since 1998.
The company operates twelve plants, the largest of which employs nine hundred people.
He filed five motions, two of which the judge dismissed before lunch. (here the of which phrase is the object of dismissed, not the subject of its clause)
entries.pronunciation note: weak: of reduces to /ə/, giving /ˌɔl ə ˈwɪtʃ/ — the stress sits on which
entries.русский: все из которых, некоторые из которых, ни один из которых — партитив о вещах
entries.case: object of of
entries.register: neutral, leaning written
entries.type: quantifier + partitive relative pronoun
entries.person / number: third person. The number of the verb is set by the quantifier when the quantifier is one that fixes number on its own (one, each, either, neither → singular; both, several, many, few → plural) and by the antecedent when it is not (all, some, most). None belongs to neither list: it goes either way, and both the singular and the plural verb are standard.
entries.refers to: things, animals, and abstractions gathered in a set. People take of whom. The antecedent is a plural or a mass noun phrase.
entries.agreement: four classes, and it is worth keeping them apart. Always singular — one of which is broken, each of which is numbered, either of which works, neither of which was under warranty; were is common in speech after neither, but careful writing keeps the singular. Always plural — both of which were returned, several of which have failed, few of which survive, many of which are duplicates. Number taken from the antecedent — all, some, and most agree with what they refer back to, so a plural count antecedent gives a plural verb (the boxes, all of which were wet; the pages, most of which are missing) and a mass antecedent gives a singular one (two tons of gravel, most of which was washed away; the testimony, some of which was sealed). Either way — none of which takes a singular or a plural verb and both are fully standard: the singular presses the "not one" reading (none of which was mentioned), the plural is the commoner choice in edited American prose (none of which were mentioned).
entries.pattern: [noun phrase], [quantifier] of which [verb] … · [noun phrase], [quantifier] of which [subject] [verb] … · [number or superlative] of which — three of which, the largest of which · always after a comma: this construction is nonrestrictive by nature
entries.contrast: of which for things against of whom for people is the only distinction that matters inside the frame, and it is absolute. What actually goes wrong is punctuation: writers reach for of them instead and produce a comma splice — ✗ He made three promises, none of them were kept. Fix it either by relativizing (none of which were kept) or by breaking the sentence (; none of them were kept). Note also that that is impossible here: ✗ three of that.
entries.see also: which, of which, both of whom, several of whom, many of whom, by which, in which, on which

entries.term: both of whom, several of whom, many of whom
entries.ipa: /ˌboʊθ əv ˈhum/, /ˈsɛvrəl əv ˈhum/, /ˌmɛni əv ˈhum/
entries.meaning: The people-side twin of all of which — a quantifier reaching back into a group and commenting on part of it.
examples: He has two sisters, both of whom live in Portland.
The panel included six economists, several of whom had advised the previous administration.
She interviewed thirty veterans, many of whom had never talked about the war to anyone.
They hired two contractors, neither of whom was licensed in this state.
The seminar has forty students, each of whom has to present twice.
He named four people in the deposition, one of whom is now his boss.
The firm has three partners, two of whom the client has never met. (here the of whom phrase is the object of met, not the subject of its clause)
entries.pronunciation note: weak: of goes to /ə/ and whom often loses its /h/ — /ˌboʊθ ə ˈum/
entries.русский: оба из которых, несколько из которых, многие из которых — партитив о людях
entries.case: object of of
entries.register: neutral to formal — the one frame in which ordinary American writing still uses whom without self-consciousness
entries.type: quantifier + partitive relative pronoun
entries.person / number: third person, people only; a plural antecedent, or exactly two for both, neither, and either
entries.refers to: human antecedents only. Things take of which.
entries.agreement: the same four classes as with of which. Always plural — both of whom were hired, several of whom have left, many of whom were veterans, few of whom remember it. Always singular — each of whom is responsible, one of whom is now his boss, either of whom is qualified, neither of whom was licensed; were is common in speech, the singular is what careful writing uses. Number taken from the antecedent — all and most of whom agree with the group they point back at, which with people is a plural count noun and therefore a plural verb (the volunteers, all of whom were interviewed; the tenants, most of whom have lived here for years). Either way — none of whom takes a singular or a plural verb, exactly as none of which does, and both are standard.
entries.pattern: [plural person noun], [quantifier] of whom [verb] … · [plural person noun], [quantifier] of whom [subject] [verb] … · [number] of whom — two of whom · always after a comma; the clause is nonrestrictive
entries.contrast: ✗ of who is an error — after a preposition the object form is required, and this is precisely the position where speakers who never otherwise say whom still say it. ✗ of that is impossible. And the comma-splice trap is identical to the of which one: ✗ I called four references, two of them never called back needs two of whom never called back, or a semicolon.
entries.see also: whom, all of which, some of which, none of which, who, to whom, for whom, with whom

entries.term: by which, in which, on which
entries.meaning: A preposition dragged to the front of the clause along with its relative pronoun — the formal alternative to leaving it stranded at the end.
examples: The speed at which the fire moved caught everyone off guard.
This is the shelf on which the original negatives were stored.
He described the process by which the bones are cleaned and cataloged.
There were four grounds on which the appeal could have been filed, and she used none of them.
The room in which we waited had one window and no clock.
The manner in which the vote was taken is now itself under review.
The meeting ran until eleven, after which nobody had the energy to argue. (sentential — the antecedent is the whole preceding clause, not a noun in it)
entries.pronunciation note: weak: the preposition reduces (/ən ˈwɪtʃ/, /ət ˈwɪtʃ/) while which keeps the stress
entries.русский: которым, в котором, на котором — предлог перед which, о вещах и местах
entries.case: object of the preposition
entries.register: formal to neutral; the stranded version is the ordinary spoken equivalent
entries.type: pied-piped preposition + relative pronoun
entries.person / number: invariant, third person
entries.refers to: things, places, times, processes, and abstractions. People take to whom, for whom, with whom. When the antecedent is a place or a time, where and when usually do the same job with less machinery: the town in which he grew up = the town where he grew up.
entries.agreement: none of its own; the verb agrees with the relative clause's own subject — the rate at which prices rise, the terms on which they were hired.
entries.pattern: [noun] [preposition] which [subject] [verb] — the drawer in which I keep it · the stranded twin: [noun] [that / Ø] [subject] [verb] … [preposition] — the drawer I keep it in · [clause], [preposition] which [subject] [verb] — sentential, as in …, after which nobody spoke
entries.contrast: Pied-piping (carrying the preposition to the front) against stranding (leaving it at the end) is a register choice, not a correctness one. Both are correct English; stranding is the unmarked American option in speech and most writing, and the belief that a clause may not end with a preposition is a seventeenth-century invention based on a Latin analogy that does not hold. The real constraint runs the other way: with that and with the zero relative, stranding is the only option, since ✗ the drawer in that I keep it is impossible. So pied-piping forces you into which or whom, and stranding opens the whole field back up.
entries.see also: which, of which, to whom, for whom, with whom, zero relative, whereupon, whereon, whereto, wherewith, whereat, whereunto, wherein, whereby, where, when

entries.meaning: The heavy, formal genitive of which — a possessive relative built out of a preposition instead of an inflection.
examples: It's an old contract, the terms of which nobody in the office can explain.
They bought a warehouse the roof of which had already partly collapsed.
The report makes forty recommendations, the first of which is to fire the consultant.
She published two studies, the conclusions of which have since been retracted.
He belongs to a club the rules of which are unwritten and strictly enforced.
This is a disease the cause of which was unknown until the early 1980s.
entries.pronunciation note: weak /ə ˈwɪtʃ/ — of is almost never given its full form here
entries.русский: которого, которой — родительный падеж о вещах: the windows of which — окна которого
entries.case: object of of
entries.register: formal, and frequently stiff
entries.type: preposition + relative pronoun, doing the work of a genitive
entries.person / number: invariant, third person
entries.refers to: things and abstractions. People take of whom.
entries.agreement: the verb agrees with the head noun of the of which phrase, not with the antecedent: a building the windows of which are original; a building the roof of which is original.
entries.pattern: [noun] the [noun] of which [verb] … — a house the roof of which leaks · [noun] the [noun] of which [subject] [verb] … — a contract the terms of which nobody read · [noun], [quantifier] of which … — the partitive frame · the heavier inversion [noun] of which the [noun] [verb] is possible and rare
entries.contrast: Against whose: identical in meaning when the possessor is inanimate, and whose wins on every count of readability — a house whose roof leaks against a house the roof of which leaks. Of which earns its place in two situations: legal and technical writing, where the possessor phrase is long and precision about what modifies what matters; and after a quantifier or number (three of which, the first of which), where whose cannot be used at all.
entries.see also: whose, which, all of which, some of which, none of which, whereupon, whereon, whereto, wherewith, whereat, whereunto, of which (determiner), whereof

entries.term: to whom, for whom, with whom
entries.meaning: The one whom that survives in ordinary use, held in place by the preposition standing in front of it. ---
examples: The counselor to whom she was assigned had a six-week backlog.
He couldn't remember the name of the officer with whom he had filed the report.
These are the neighbors for whom we've been collecting mail all month.
There's a woman in accounting from whom I've learned more than from any manual.
My uncle, about whom the less said the better, showed up anyway.
The letter began "To whom it may concern," which told her everything she needed to know.
entries.pronunciation note: weak: the preposition reduces to schwa and whom can lose its /h/ at speed — /tə ˈum/
entries.русский: которому, для которого, с которым — предлог перед whom, только о людях
entries.case: object of the preposition
entries.register: formal to neutral in writing; in speech the stranded version with who or nothing is the ordinary form
entries.type: pied-piped preposition + relative pronoun; the same frame serves as an interrogative (To whom am I speaking?)
entries.person / number: invariant; people only
entries.refers to: human antecedents only. Things take to which, for which, with which.
entries.agreement: none of its own; the verb agrees with the relative clause's own subject — the neighbors for whom we collect the mail.
entries.pattern: [person noun] [preposition] whom [subject] [verb] — the agent to whom I spoke · the stranded twin: [person noun] [who / that / Ø] [subject] [verb] … [preposition] — the agent I spoke to · [person noun], [preposition] whom [subject] [verb], … — nonrestrictive · fixed phrases: to whom it may concern, for whom the bell tolls
entries.contrast: This is the last position in American English where whom is not optional: directly after a preposition it is the only correct form, and ✗ the agent to who I spoke is an error. Strand the preposition and the picture flips — the agent who I spoke to is unremarkable in speech and fine in most writing, while the agent whom I spoke to is correct but sounds like someone is being watched. Both structures are grammatical; what changes is how formal the sentence sounds and how far the preposition has traveled.
entries.see also: whom, who, by which, in which, on which, both of whom, several of whom, many of whom, zero relative

entries.meaning: The relative that needs a host: it appears only after such or the same, or as a comment on a whole clause.
examples: He offered such help as he could and then went home.
Such of the records as survive are in the county archive.
We ran into the same problems as were reported in the pilot study.
She wore the same coat as her sister had worn to the funeral.
The deadline was moved twice, as everyone expected.
As is often the case with sealed bids, the low number was the least reliable.
Them as has, gets. (nonstandard)
The man as sold me the truck has left town. (nonstandard)

senses.head: After such
examples: He offered such help as he could and then went home.
Such of the records as survive are in the county archive.

senses.head: After the same
examples: We ran into the same problems as were reported in the pilot study.
She wore the same coat as her sister had worn to the funeral.

senses.head: Sentential relative
body: The antecedent is the whole clause, and as may come before or after it.
examples: The deadline was moved twice, as everyone expected.
As is often the case with sealed bids, the low number was the least reliable.

senses.head: General relative — nonstandard
body: In older rural and working-class speech — the American South and Midland, and northern England, the English Midlands, Scotland, and Ireland — as replaces that in ordinary relative clauses. Dialect only; recognize it, do not write it. Them as has, gets carries two further nonstandard features along with the relative — the demonstrative them standing in for those, and the dialect singular verb after a plural subject (them … has).
examples: Them as has, gets. (nonstandard)
The man as sold me the truck has left town. (nonstandard)

entries.pronunciation note: weak /əz/ — the weak form is the usual one in this use, since the stress falls on such or same
entries.русский: который; как — относительное только после such и the same, а также о целом предложении
entries.case: none — it serves as subject or object of its clause
entries.register: neutral in the such and the same frames, neutral in the sentential use, nonstandard in the general-relative dialect use (rural Southern and Midland American; northern and Midland English, Scots, and Irish)
entries.type: relative pronoun after such and the same (marginally after so many, so much); elsewhere a conjunction or a preposition
entries.person / number: invariant
entries.refers to: whatever such or the same points at — people or things — and, in the sentential use, an entire clause.
entries.agreement: as subject, the verb agrees with the antecedent: such people as are willing, the same problems as were reported last year. In the sentential use the verb is singular, since the antecedent is a whole proposition: as is usual, as was expected.
entries.pattern: such [noun] as [verb] — such help as remains · such [noun] as [subject] [verb] — such help as he could offer · the same [noun] as [subject] [verb] · [clause], as [verb] — sentential: …, as was predicted · As [verb], [clause] — fronted sentential: As is often the case, …
entries.contrast: Against that after the same: both are used — the same car as I drove and the same car that I drove — and the traditional distinction is that as points to a matching item while that points to the identical one. The distinction is real but soft, and no reader will be misled either way. Against which in the sentential use: which can only follow its clause (He was late, which surprised us), while as can also come first (As we all know, he was late) and carries a flavor of "in accordance with what."
entries.see also: that, which, them that / them as / them what, such as (fused relative), such, the same as, as (comparison)

entries.meaning: The negative relative: a single word carrying both the pronoun and the not, standard in English through the nineteenth century and now confined to proverbs and period prose.
examples: There is scarcely a family in the county but has lost someone to the mine.
No one hears that recording but wonders how it survived at all.
Not a man among them but would have gone back for her.
There was not a window in the old schoolhouse but was broken.
Few of his students but remembered that lecture forty years later.
Scarcely a week passes but brings another complaint from the neighbors.
entries.pronunciation note: weak /bət/ — in this use it is unstressed and easy to miss
entries.русский: который не — устар. отрицательное относительное: no one but knows — нет никого, кто не знал бы
entries.case: none — it functions as the subject of its clause
entries.register: archaic, literary, proverbial. Read it; do not write it except in deliberate pastiche.
entries.type: negative relative pronoun, archaic and literary; elsewhere a coordinating conjunction or a preposition meaning except
entries.person / number: invariant
entries.refers to: people or things, and only when the main clause is negative or near-negative — after no one, not a, nobody, never, scarcely, few
entries.agreement: as the subject of its clause it takes a verb agreeing with the antecedent: there is no one but knows the story; there were few but knew the risk.
entries.pattern: [negative expression] but [verb] … — no man but knows · there is / was no [noun] but [verb] · the modern rewrite is who does not or that does not
entries.contrast: It means "who … not" or "that … not" all by itself — the negative is built into the word, which is why the clause that follows contains no not. Two negatives are therefore correct here and only look wrong: There is no one but knows the story means There is no one who does not know the story, that is, everybody knows it. Adding a second negative (✗ no one but doesn't know) reverses the meaning by accident. Keep it apart from the coordinating conjunction but (small but sturdy), from the preposition but meaning except (everyone but me, with the object case), from the fixed but that (I don't doubt but that he'll come), and — the one that actually gets miscounted — from the conjunction but after so: in There was never a sermon so short but someone complained, but is followed by its own subject (someone) and means "that … not," so nothing is left for a pronoun to do. The test is the one that separates relative that from complementizer that: the relative but is the subject of its clause, so the clause has no other subject. Put a noun or pronoun after it and you have left this entry — no one but her knows the whole story is the preposition but meaning except: her is its object, and the subject of knows is the whole phrase no one but her. One case note while we are here, since this is the entry where it bites: after prepositional but the object form is the ordinary American choice — everyone but me, nobody but him, no one but her — and the older no one but she knows, in which the pronoun copies the case of no one because but is being read as a conjunction, is a formal variant rather than an error. What is not a variant is the coordination rule the opening section of this file is built on: but is a preposition here, so ✗ everyone but my wife and I is the same hypercorrection as ✗ between you and I, and the deletion test settles it — everyone but me → everyone but my wife and me.
entries.see also: that, who, but (archaic conjunction), but that

entries.meaning: A whole relative clause frozen into a cross-reference: which is the object, see is an imperative, and the two words together say "go look this one up in this same book." Latin wrote it quod vide, American reference works abbreviate it q.v., and almost nobody spells the English out any more.
examples: The doctrine descends from the old writ of assumpsit (q.v.).
Her early canvases owe everything to the Nabis (q.v.), and she never quite admitted it.
At a distance the bird is regularly mistaken for the northern harrier (q.v.).
On the history of the tenure, see the entry for seisin, q.v.
The whole argument turns on the older meaning of consideration, q.v.
The reader should consult the entries for estoppel and laches (qq.v.) before going further.
The style begins with the Aesthetic Movement, which see, and ends in the poster art of the nineties. (dated)
Compare the entry Habeas Corpus, which see, for the procedural history. (dated)
The doctrine descends from the old writ of assumpsit; see "Assumpsit," page 214. (the modern rewrite of example 1)
See also the entries for estoppel and laches. (the modern rewrite of example 6)

senses.head: The standard parenthetical
body: Directly after the term, inside parentheses, with no comma between the term and the parenthesis and none after the abbreviation.
examples: The doctrine descends from the old writ of assumpsit (q.v.).
Her early canvases owe everything to the Nabis (q.v.), and she never quite admitted it.
At a distance the bird is regularly mistaken for the northern harrier (q.v.).

senses.head: Unparenthesized, after a comma
body: Older, slightly more literary, and it closes the sentence rather than sitting inside it.
examples: On the history of the tenure, see the entry for seisin, q.v.
The whole argument turns on the older meaning of consideration, q.v.

senses.head: The plural qq.v
body: Two or more cross-references pointed at in one breath.
examples: The reader should consult the entries for estoppel and laches (qq.v.) before going further.

senses.head: The English gloss written out
body: Which see — the calque, and the shape that makes the grammar visible: a relative pronoun standing as the object of an imperative verb.
examples: The style begins with the Aesthetic Movement, which see, and ends in the poster art of the nineties. (dated)
Compare the entry Habeas Corpus, which see, for the procedural history. (dated)

senses.head: What an American editor writes instead
body: The reason this is a reading item rather than a writing one.
examples: The doctrine descends from the old writ of assumpsit; see "Assumpsit," page 214. (the modern rewrite of example 1)
See also the entries for estoppel and laches. (the modern rewrite of example 6)

entries.pronunciation note: the abbreviation is read out as its two letter names and never as the Latin behind it. The unabbreviated quod vide is /kwɑd ˈwiˌdeɪ/ in the restored classical pronunciation and /kwɑd ˈvaɪdi/ kwod-VY-dee in the traditional English pronunciation of Latin, which is what an older American lawyer or librarian says. The English gloss which see is /ˌwɪtʃ ˈsi/ wich-SEE, and it does have a weak form: which is unstressed in the phrase and reduces to /wətʃ/, giving /wətʃ ˈsi/ with every bit of the stress on see. The plural qq.v. is /ˌkju ˌkju ˈvi/. The abbreviation itself has no weak form, since it is spelled out letter by letter.
entries.русский: см. там же — книжн. отсылка к статье в той же книге; по-русски просто «см.»
entries.case: object — which is what see takes, which is the whole grammatical point of the phrase and the reason the Latin uses accusative quod rather than nominative quid
entries.register: formal, scholarly, and dated. Its home is the reference work — encyclopedias, dictionaries, gazetteers, legal and scientific treatises, and the scholarly editions of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, where an American student still meets it constantly. American editing now prefers plain see with a page number, or a link; which see written out reads as deliberate antiquing.
entries.type: a relative clause frozen into a cross-reference formula — which is the object of the imperative see, fronted ahead of its own verb, so the two words together mean "see this one." Q.v. abbreviates Latin quod vide, in which quod is the same relative pronoun standing in the accusative. Style manuals file it with the Latin reference tags; it is entered here because the word inside it is a genuine relative pronoun with its antecedent sitting in the sentence
entries.person / number: invariant, third person, with no number of its own. Latin marks the plural — qq.v., for quae vide, when two or more terms are being pointed at — but the English which see never changes shape: the hen harrier and the marsh harrier, which see.
entries.refers to: the term just named, of whatever kind — a word, a person, a place, a doctrine, a species, a movement. The antecedent is always the noun phrase immediately in front of it, never a whole clause (that is ordinary sentential which) and never the reader being addressed. And it points inside the same work: q.v. is a promise that this book has an entry of its own for the term.
entries.agreement: none whatever. Which is an object here, so it never controls a verb, and the verb it belongs to is an imperative, which does not inflect for person or number. Which see stays which see after a singular antecedent, a plural one, or two of them at once — never ✗ which sees, never ✗ which are seen.
entries.pattern: [term] (q.v.) — the standard shape: parentheses, immediately after the term, no comma inside · [term], q.v. — unparenthesized, after a comma, closing the sentence · [term] and [term] (qq.v.) — the plural, for two cross-references at once · [term], which see — the English gloss written out · see [term] — the modern rewrite · never ✗ separated from its antecedent by intervening words · never ✗ followed by a comma when it stands inside parentheses
entries.contrast: Against cf. (Latin confer, "compare"): cf. sends you to something that differs from what you have just read and asks you to notice the difference, while q.v. tells you that the work in your hands has its own entry for the term just named. Against ibid. and op. cit., which point back at a source already cited rather than sideways at an entry in the same book. Against ordinary relative which: the pronoun and its object function are identical, but everything around it is frozen — the verb is fixed in the imperative, nothing can be added to the clause, and no substitution is available, so ✗ that see and ✗ whom see are impossible and the zero relative is impossible too, the pronoun being the only thing doing the pointing. Against the entry in the conjunction dictionary: same phrase, different question — quod vide covers the punctuation and the company it keeps (i.e., e.g., cf., n.b.), while this entry covers the relative pronoun inside it.
entries.variants: qq.v. (plural, from Latin quae vide); the unabbreviated quod vide; the English calque which see; and the plain modern instructions see, see also, and see under. The vide of it — the imperative "see" — is the same verb that gives vide supra ("see above"), vide infra ("see below"), and videlicet (viz., "namely").
entries.see also: which, that, of which, the which, what (fused relative), quod vide, confer, videlicet, nota bene, id est, exempli gratia

entries.meaning: A fused relative assembled out of two ordinary words: such carries the antecedent, as does the relative work, and the pair stands where a whole noun phrase would.
examples: Such as wish to be heard should sign the sheet by the door before nine. (formal)
Such as survive of the original letters are kept in the county archive.
He talked to such as would listen, and there were never many of them.
He gave such as he had and apologized for the rest.
She wrote down such as she could remember of the conversation.
The furniture, such as it is, comes with the apartment.
Her savings, such as they are, won't cover one semester.
The contractor shall replace such as are found defective within thirty days. (drafting)

senses.head: Fused subject of its own clause
body: The commonest shape, and the one that sounds most like a proclamation.
examples: Such as wish to be heard should sign the sheet by the door before nine. (formal)
Such as survive of the original letters are kept in the county archive.
He talked to such as would listen, and there were never many of them.

senses.head: Fused object of its own clause
body: The gap is inside the clause rather than in front of it.
examples: He gave such as he had and apologized for the rest.
She wrote down such as she could remember of the conversation.

senses.head: The fixed such as it is
body: A concession hung on a noun already named — "for what little it is worth." The verb agrees with the pronoun inside the phrase, so a plural referent gives such as they are.
examples: The furniture, such as it is, comes with the apartment.
Her savings, such as they are, won't cover one semester.

senses.head: In legal drafting
body: Still written, and the reason a paralegal meets the construction at all.
examples: The contractor shall replace such as are found defective within thirty days. (drafting)

entries.pronunciation note: weak: as is /əz/ here and never the strong /æz/, since the stress sits on such; the fixed phrase runs together as /ˌsʌtʃ əz ɪt ˈɪz/ such as it is
entries.русский: те, кто; то, что — книжн. слитное относительное без антецедента: such as remain — те, кто остался
entries.case: none; the phrase as a whole serves as subject, object, or complement, and as inside the clause is that clause's own subject or object
entries.register: formal, legal, and literary, archaic-leaning in speech. The productive use (such as wish to attend) is nineteenth-century in flavor; what survives in ordinary American English is the fixed concessive such as it is / such as they are and the drafting formula such as may be required.
entries.type: fused relative — such supplies the antecedent and as does the relative work, so the two words together fill a noun slot
entries.person / number: invariant, third person. Plural by default, since the fused antecedent is normally a set — such as remain = those that remain; singular only when the reference is to a mass or to a single thing.
entries.refers to: people and things alike, and always by fused reference: no antecedent stands anywhere in the sentence for the phrase to point back at, because such carries its own inside it. Such as wish to be heard = those who wish to be heard; such as survive = the ones that survive.
entries.agreement: the verb inside the clause is plural whenever the fused antecedent is a set of countable people or things — such as are willing, such as remain, such as were left behind — and singular when it is a mass or a single item: such as is needed, such as was left of the estate. In the fixed phrase the verb follows the pronoun sitting inside it: such as it is, such as they are.
entries.pattern: such as [verb] … — fused subject: such as remain · such as [subject] [verb] — fused object: such as he could offer · [verb] such as [subject] [modal] [verb] — drafting: furnish such as may be required · such as it is, such as they are — fixed, appended to a noun already given · never ✗ such as [noun] in this sense: with a noun after it the phrase is the everyday "for example" one, and not a relative at all
entries.contrast: Against the everyday such as meaning "for example" — a citrus fruit such as a lemon — the test is what comes next. A noun phrase after it means "for example," and there is an antecedent sitting in front of it; a bare verb, or a subject and a verb, means the fused relative, and there is no antecedent anywhere in the sentence. Against as in this file: plain relative as needs a noun for such to modify (such help as he could give), while in the fused version the noun is gone and such stands on its own (such as he could give). Against those who and those that: those are the modern equivalents, and unless the period flavor is the point they make the better sentence — Such as wish to attend is Those who wish to attend. Against the other fused relatives, what and whoever: the mechanism is identical and only the coverage differs — what fuses "the thing that," whoever fuses "anyone who," and such as fuses "those who" with an added sense of "as many of them as there are." And the legal such of such defects and such party is a determiner, since a noun has to follow it; it belongs to the determiner dictionary and is not this entry.
entries.variants: such … as with the noun left in (such records as survive) is the unfused parent construction and is treated at as; such of … as (such of the records as survive) is the partitive version of the same thing.
entries.see also: as, that, which, such (quantifying pronoun), such (demonstrative pronoun), what (fused relative), whoever, such (determiner), the same as, fused relatives

entries.meaning: The last relative use of than: a fossil that ranks the person just named above everyone else in the field, in two words and a pair of commas.
examples: The chair called on Dr. Whitfield, than whom nobody in the room had read the file more closely.
She learned the trade from an old pressman, than whom no one alive knew more about lead type.
The prize goes to Ellen Park, than whom this department has produced no finer teacher.
He dedicated the book to his mother, than whom he had known no more patient reader.
The bridge, than which few structures in the state have aged better, reopened last spring.
They cut the one paragraph, than which nothing in the draft had cost more argument.
He signed off as "your obedient servant, than whom none is more obedient," and thought it was very funny.
Readers usually meet the construction in Milton, where Beelzebub is the one than whom, Satan excepted, none higher sat.

senses.head: Ranking a person above all others
body: The core use, and the reason the phrase survives at all.
examples: The chair called on Dr. Whitfield, than whom nobody in the room had read the file more closely.
She learned the trade from an old pressman, than whom no one alive knew more about lead type.

senses.head: In a tribute or a citation
body: Award programs, endowed chairs, and eulogies keep it in print.
examples: The prize goes to Ellen Park, than whom this department has produced no finer teacher.
He dedicated the book to his mother, than whom he had known no more patient reader.

senses.head: The inanimate variant than which
body: Same frame, different antecedent, and rarer still.
examples: The bridge, than which few structures in the state have aged better, reopened last spring.
They cut the one paragraph, than which nothing in the draft had cost more argument.

senses.head: As deliberate archaism
body: Modern writers reach for it when they want the eighteenth century in the room, or when they are joking.
examples: He signed off as "your obedient servant, than whom none is more obedient," and thought it was very funny.
Readers usually meet the construction in Milton, where Beelzebub is the one than whom, Satan excepted, none higher sat.

entries.pronunciation note: weak /ðən ˈhum/ — than is unstressed in this phrase and reduces to /ðən/ or to syllabic /ðn̩/, and whom drops its /h/ at speed, giving /ðən ˈum/. The full /ðæn/ turns up only when someone is reading the phrase aloud as a curiosity.
entries.русский: лучше которого никто — устар. книжн. оборот превосходства о человеке
entries.case: object of than
entries.register: formal, literary, and frankly archaic. Milton and Johnson wrote it; an American meets it today in tributes, award citations, obituaries, and jokes about tributes, award citations, and obituaries.
entries.type: fossilized preposition + relative pronoun — the one construction in modern English where than is unmistakably a preposition taking an object
entries.person / number: invariant; people only. The antecedent may be singular or plural — a scholar than whom, two editors than whom — and whom does not change either way.
entries.refers to: a human antecedent just named and now being ranked against everyone else in its class. The clause always carries a comparison, and almost always a negative that turns the comparison into a superlative: than whom no one is better qualified. The inanimate counterpart is than which (see Variants); otherwise things take an ordinary comparative — a tower higher than any other, not a relative clause.
entries.agreement: none of its own. As the object of than it never controls a verb; the verb of the clause agrees with that clause's own subject, which is normally the negative quantifier — a scholar than whom none was more careful, two editors than whom none were stricter.
entries.pattern: [person noun], than whom [no one / nobody / none / few] [verb] [comparative], [rest of the main clause] · [person noun], than whom [subject] [verb] [no one / nothing] more, … · the inanimate twin: [noun], than which [nothing / few] [verb] [comparative], … · commas on both sides, always — the clause is supplementary and can never be restrictive · never ✗ than who · never as a free relative: ✗ than whom I spoke to
entries.contrast: This is the sentence that keeps the than argument alive. Read as a conjunction, than introduces a clause and a pronoun after it takes subject case — He is taller than I am, and elliptically than I. Read as a preposition, it takes an object — He is taller than me, which is ordinary standard American English and not an error. Than whom exists only on the prepositional reading: nobody has ever written ✗ than who, which is why the phrase gets quoted in every argument about the word. Against to whom, for whom, with whom: those frames are living, productive, and neutral in register, and they will take any clause you put after them; than whom is one frozen shape with the comparison built into it and no other use. Against the plain modern sentence: a scholar than whom none was more careful is a scholar more careful than anyone else, and outside deliberate formality the plain version is the better one.
entries.variants: than which — the same fossil with an inanimate antecedent (a doctrine than which nothing was more contested), rarer still, and the only way the construction will accept a thing.
entries.see also: whom, who, to whom, for whom, with whom, both of whom, several of whom, many of whom, than whom (conjunction dictionary), than, personal pronoun case

entries.meaning: The medieval definite-article form of which, kept alive only by the texts that were written before it died.
examples: He left her a farm, the which she sold within the year.
They came at last to a river, the which they could not cross before nightfall.
She spoke of a promise, the which he had long since forgotten.
It was a law of long standing, by the which many a family had been ruined.
He carried a letter, the which he would show to no one.
There stood a chapel, in the which the family had been buried for three centuries.
entries.русский: который — устар. форма which с артиклем, из Библии короля Якова и Шекспира
entries.case: none
entries.register: archaic — common from Middle English through the seventeenth century, then gone. It survives in the King James Bible, in Shakespeare, and in deliberate antiquing.
entries.type: archaic relative pronoun
entries.person / number: invariant
entries.refers to: things chiefly, and people in the older texts, from the period when plain which could still take a human antecedent (Our Father which art in heaven)
entries.agreement: the verb agrees with the antecedent, exactly as with plain which
entries.pattern: [noun] the which [verb] … · [noun] [preposition] the which [subject] [verb] — by the which he was condemned
entries.contrast: Nothing separates it from plain which except four hundred years. The article is a leftover from a period when which still patterned like a noun and could take a determiner in front of it — the same instinct that produced the determiner the which (the which cause). It is a reading item, not a writing item, and using it in modern prose reads as costume.
entries.see also: which, the which (determiner), whereof

entries.term: them that / them as / them what
entries.meaning: Those who, with the dialect demonstrative them as the head and any of three relatives hung on it. One frame, three fillers, and an honest split running through it: in the object slot it is period-standard English, in the subject slot it is dialect. Like most dialect material it does not travel alone, and the examples below carry the nonstandard -s verb and, in one case, negative concord along with the pronoun; each is labeled.
examples: Them that has, gets. (nonstandard — proverbial; the dialect -s verb rides along with the pronoun)
Them that come late don't get fed. (nonstandard)
Them that wrote the rules never had to live under them. (nonstandard)
Them as knows, knows. (nonstandard)
Them as wants seconds can go around again. (nonstandard)
Them what pays the piper calls the tune. (nonstandard)
Them what ain't got nothing got nothing to lose. (nonstandard — negative concord riding along: ain't … nothing is a single negation in these varieties, not two)
"The LORD pitieth them that fear him." (Psalm 103:13, King James Version — object of pitieth, and standard for its period)
"Remember them that are in bonds, as bound with them." (Hebrews 13:3, King James Version)
The fund was set up for them that had lost everything in the fire. (dated in flavor, but the case is ordinary)
"Them that has, gets" — which is the whole theory of the tax code in four words. (quoting the proverb)

senses.head: them that — the fused subject
body: The commonest of the three, and the one an American will actually hear.
examples: Them that has, gets. (nonstandard — proverbial; the dialect -s verb rides along with the pronoun)
Them that come late don't get fed. (nonstandard)
Them that wrote the rules never had to live under them. (nonstandard)

senses.head: them as — Southern and Midland American, and northern British
body: The relative as doing the work that does elsewhere.
examples: Them as knows, knows. (nonstandard)
Them as wants seconds can go around again. (nonstandard)

senses.head: them what — the heaviest marked of the three
body: Cockney and southern English dialect writing above all, and American dialect writing after it.
examples: Them what pays the piper calls the tune. (nonstandard)
Them what ain't got nothing got nothing to lose. (nonstandard — negative concord riding along: ain't … nothing is a single negation in these varieties, not two)

senses.head: In the object slot, where it is not dialect at all
body: After a verb or a preposition the head is simply in the case the sentence calls for. This is the archaic-but-standard use, and the King James Bible is where an American meets it.
examples: "The LORD pitieth them that fear him." (Psalm 103:13, King James Version — object of pitieth, and standard for its period)
"Remember them that are in bonds, as bound with them." (Hebrews 13:3, King James Version)
The fund was set up for them that had lost everything in the fire. (dated in flavor, but the case is ordinary)

senses.head: Quoted by standard speakers
body: The proverb travels much further than the dialect does, and people who would never say them for those produce this one intact.
examples: "Them that has, gets" — which is the whole theory of the tax code in four words. (quoting the proverb)

entries.pronunciation note: the weak forms are what a listener actually gets, because the whole phrase is unstressed machinery sitting in front of the verb that carries the point: them reduces to /ðəm/ and after a consonant to /əm/, and the relative reduces with it, giving /ðəm ðət/, /ðəm əz/, /ðəm wət/. Them that has, gets comes out /ðəm ət ˈhæz ˈɡɛts/ at speed, which is why dialect writing spells it them 'at has. Do not read the reduction as the dialect: the /əm/ of I saw 'em is ordinary General American and marks nothing at all.
entries.русский: те, кто — прост., диал. вместо those who; в роли подлежащего нестандартно
entries.case: the head them is historically the object form of they, and the dialect use puts it in subject position as well (Them that has, gets); the relative itself has no case
entries.register: nonstandard as a subject, and the region differs by member. Them that is the widest — Southern and South Midland American, Appalachian, and rural and working-class speech generally, plus African American English; it is the version an American is most likely to hear spoken. Them as carries the dialect relative as, which belongs to the American South and Midland and, in Britain, to northern England, the English Midlands, Scotland, and Ireland; an American now meets it mostly in print — Hardy, George Eliot, Lawrence — and in older rural speech. Them what is the most heavily marked of the three, the stock form of Cockney and southern English dialect writing (Dickens, the music hall) and of American dialect writing after it (Twain, Faulkner). In the object slot the same string is not dialect at all: see the Contrast.
entries.type: fused-relative frame, nonstandard in its main use — the dialect demonstrative them standing in for those as the head, with a relative pronoun hung on it; the three members differ only in which relative fills the slot, and all three mean those who
entries.person / number: third person plural, and generic rather than pointing at anyone in particular. The singular members of the same frame — him that, her that, he that — are archaic rather than regional.
entries.refers to: people, almost always: an open class of them, whoever does or has what the relative clause says. Things turn up occasionally (them that's left over go back in the box), but the frame is built for persons. It is never used for one identified individual; for that these same varieties say the one that.
entries.agreement: two things are going on at once and only one of them belongs to the pronoun. The relative clause normally takes the -s form of the verb whatever the number — them that has, them as knows, them what wants — which is dialect verb agreement (the Northern Subject Rule and its American descendants) riding along with the pronoun, not a fact about them. The main clause follows the same varieties' habits: Them that comes late gets nothing. The standard equivalent is plural throughout: those who have, those who come late get nothing.
entries.pattern: them that / them as / them what [verb] … + [main verb] — the fused subject, and the marked use · [verb or preposition] them that [verb] — the object slot: for them that mourn · them that's — with is or has contracted onto the relative · the standard rewrites: those who, those that, the ones who, whoever · never ✗ them + [noun] in this entry: put a noun after it (them apples, them boxes) and them is a determiner, which belongs to the determiner dictionary and not here
entries.contrast: Three separate things get run together here, and they come apart cleanly. Position decides the label. Them that in the object slot — the Lord pitieth them that fear him, a fund for them that lost everything — is the object case doing exactly what an object case should, and it is period-standard English rather than dialect: it is the oblique member of the old he that / they that frame, ordinary through the seventeenth century, preserved in the King James Bible, and dated but never regional today. Them that in the subject slot (Them that has, gets) puts an object form where a subject belongs, and that is the nonstandard part — the same shape of thing as ✗ Me and him went, and marked for the same reason. The head is not the relative. What is nonstandard in them that is them, standing in for those; the that is the ordinary standard relative of this whole file. In them as and them what both halves are marked, since as and what are themselves dialect relatives, which is why those two sound heavier. The pronunciation is not the use. Reduced /əm/ is standard American speech; demonstrative them is not. Against those who and those that: those are the standard equivalents in every register, and they are what an editor will write. Against he who, he that, she who, they that: the identical frame with a nominative head, archaic rather than dialect. Against whoever: the living one-word equivalent — Them that wants seconds is Whoever wants seconds.
entries.variants: them 'at (eye-dialect spelling of the reduced that); them as what and them what has with a doubled relative, in the broadest varieties; the singular him that and her that; and the standard and archaic members of the same frame — he that, they that, those that, those who — treated at he that and those who.
entries.see also: that, as, what (nonstandard relative), zero relative, them, them there, those who, those which, them (dialectal demonstrative), them'uns, he who, he that, she who, they that, whoever, nothing (negative concord), them (determiner), he that

entries.meaning: The all-purpose relative of several English dialects, included here so a reader recognizes it on the page and knows what it is doing. Dialect rarely arrives one feature at a time, and four of the examples below carry a second marked form along with the relative: them boxes is the nonstandard demonstrative them for those, he done it is the dialect past tense of do, I told you about him leaves a resumptive pronoun sitting in the gap the relative was supposed to empty, and ain't nobody … nothing is negative concord — the double negative, in which each further negative agrees with the first instead of canceling it, systematic in Southern, Appalachian, and African American English and nonstandard in edited American prose. All four are labeled, and none of them is a typo.
examples: The fella what fixed my truck moved to Tulsa. (nonstandard)
That's the woman what called about the dog. (nonstandard)
It was my own brother what told them where to look. (nonstandard)
Every man what worked that shift got sick inside a week. (nonstandard)
The truck what he sold me broke down inside a month. (nonstandard — what is the object of sold)
The only thing what she kept was her mother's ring. (nonstandard)
Them boxes what came yesterday are still sitting on the porch. (nonstandard — them for those)
He's the one what done it, and everybody knew it. (nonstandard — done for did)
There ain't nobody around here what knows nothing about it. (nonstandard — negative concord: ain't … nobody … nothing is a single negation in these varieties, not three)
