That's the man what I told you about him. (nonstandard)

senses.head: Subject of its own clause
body: The commonest shape by far.
examples: The fella what fixed my truck moved to Tulsa. (nonstandard)
That's the woman what called about the dog. (nonstandard)
It was my own brother what told them where to look. (nonstandard)
Every man what worked that shift got sick inside a week. (nonstandard)

senses.head: Object of its own clause
body: The same one word, doing the job standard English splits between that, which, whom, and nothing.
examples: The truck what he sold me broke down inside a month. (nonstandard — what is the object of sold)
The only thing what she kept was her mother's ring. (nonstandard)

senses.head: Carrying another dialect feature along
examples: Them boxes what came yesterday are still sitting on the porch. (nonstandard — them for those)
He's the one what done it, and everybody knew it. (nonstandard — done for did)
There ain't nobody around here what knows nothing about it. (nonstandard — negative concord: ain't … nobody … nothing is a single negation in these varieties, not three)

senses.head: With a resumptive pronoun
body: The broadest varieties fill the gap back in instead of leaving it open.
examples: That's the man what I told you about him. (nonstandard)

entries.pronunciation note: weak /wət/ — unstressed and usually reduced in this use
entries.русский: который — прост., диал. вместо that: the man what owns the place; в грамотной речи недопустимо
entries.case: none — subject or object of its clause
entries.register: nonstandard. Regional and working-class speech — Southern, Appalachian, and other rural American varieties; in Britain, Cockney, East Anglian, and other southern English ones — together with the dialect writing that records it (Twain, Faulkner, Cockney and Southern dialogue). Never correct in edited prose.
entries.type: relative pronoun, nonstandard
entries.person / number: invariant
entries.refers to: people and things alike, exactly like the that it replaces
entries.agreement: as subject, the verb agrees with the antecedent: the man what owns the place; and in the dialects that use it, nonstandard agreement often comes along with it (the men what owns the place)
entries.pattern: [noun] what [verb] … · [noun] what [subject] [verb] … · in the broadest varieties, doubled with a resumptive pronoun: the man what I told you about him
entries.contrast: Do not confuse it with the fused relative what, which is completely standard: I heard what you said means the thing that you said, and what carries its own antecedent inside it. The tell is simple — the nonstandard relative has an antecedent sitting right in front of it (the thing what you said), and the fused relative has none. Standard English uses that, which, who, or nothing in the slot this dialect what fills; the dialect uses one word for all four, which is why it is so easy to understand and so unmistakably marked.
entries.see also: that, zero relative, which, them that / them as / them what, what (relative determiner), what (fused relative), whatever, them (nonstandard demonstrative), fused relatives

entries.term: whereupon, whereon, whereto, wherewith, whereat, whereunto
entries.meaning: Six survivals of a pattern that was once general: where- welded onto a preposition to make a single word meaning "[preposition] which." Five of them are words to read rather than to write. Whereupon is still in use.
examples: The witness refused a third time, whereupon the judge cleared the courtroom.
She named a figure, whereupon the whole table went quiet.
The chairman ruled her out of order, whereat half the room stood up and left. (archaic)
The land whereon the mill stood has been a parking lot since 1961. (archaic, legal)
Exhibit C is the schedule whereto the easement description is attached. (archaic, legal)
They were left with nothing wherewith to pay the workmen. (archaic)
He had the plans for the house but never the money wherewith to build it. (archaic)
He was ordained to the ministry whereunto he believed himself called. (archaic)
The trust names the purposes whereunto its income may be applied. (archaic, legal)

senses.head: whereupon — immediate sequence
body: The living member, and the one to punctuate carefully: it is a relative, not a conjunctive adverb, so it takes a comma before it and can never begin a sentence.
examples: The witness refused a third time, whereupon the judge cleared the courtroom.
She named a figure, whereupon the whole table went quiet.

senses.head: whereat — the reaction
body: Archaic-literary: at which point, with the sense that somebody responded to what just happened.
examples: The chairman ruled her out of order, whereat half the room stood up and left. (archaic)

senses.head: whereon and whereto — place, and destination
body: Deeds, wills, and land descriptions, plus the scriptural echo.
examples: The land whereon the mill stood has been a parking lot since 1961. (archaic, legal)
Exhibit C is the schedule whereto the easement description is attached. (archaic, legal)

senses.head: wherewith — the means, and usually the missing means
body: Nearly always followed by to and an infinitive.
examples: They were left with nothing wherewith to pay the workmen. (archaic)
He had the plans for the house but never the money wherewith to build it. (archaic)

senses.head: whereunto — the King James register
body: A purpose, an office, or a calling that something is directed toward.
examples: He was ordained to the ministry whereunto he believed himself called. (archaic)
The trust names the purposes whereunto its income may be applied. (archaic, legal)

entries.pronunciation note: and whereunto /ˌwɛrənˈtu/, wair-un-TOO. The stress falls on the preposition in every one of them, never on where-, and wherewith is heard with either /θ/ or /ð/. Weak forms: the first syllable reduces in running speech to /wɚ/ — whereupon /ˌwɚəˈpɑn/, whereat /wɚˈæt/ — which is why these words slide past a listener when a clerk is reading minutes aloud.
entries.русский: на котором, к которому, чем — устар., юр. сращения «where- + предлог»; whereupon «после чего»
entries.case: none — the where- element is the object of the attached preposition, but nothing inflects
entries.register: archaic to legal, and it differs word by word. Whereupon is the live one: "and immediately after that," ordinary in court transcripts, board minutes, and formal narrative, and the only member an American is likely to write. Whereat is archaic-literary, the reaction word of nineteenth-century fiction. Whereon, whereto, and wherewith are archaic outside deeds, wills, and scriptural echo — the King James Bible of 1611 and the prose written in imitation of it. Whereunto is the deadest of the six; the -unto shape survives in American English only in its demonstrative cousin hereunto, still typed into signature blocks (have hereunto set their hands).
entries.type: relative pro-adverbs — where- stands in for the relative and the welded preposition governs it, so each word is exactly one pied-piped preposition plus which: whereon = on which, whereto = to which, wherewith = with which, whereat = at which, whereunto = unto which, whereupon = upon which. Grammars are divided over whether to file them as pronouns or as adverbs; they are entered here because they fill exactly the slot by which, in which, on which fills, and each one's full treatment as a connector is in the conjunction dictionary
entries.person / number: invariant. No person, no number, no case, nothing to inflect.
entries.refers to: things, places, documents, and abstractions — and, for whereupon and whereat, a whole preceding clause together with the event it names. Never a person — ✗ the man whereto I wrote; people take to whom. In drafting the antecedent is normally a document or one of its parts — the schedule whereto the exhibits are attached.
entries.agreement: none of its own; the verb agrees with the subject of the clause the word introduces — the terms whereon the parties have agreed, the table whereon the papers lie. With whereupon the antecedent is the whole preceding clause, and the clause that follows brings its own subject: …, whereupon the meeting adjourned.
entries.pattern: [noun] whereon / whereto / wherewith / whereunto [subject] [verb] — the rock whereon it stands · [noun] wherewith / whereon to [verb] — no money wherewith to pay · [clause], whereupon [subject] [verb] — the living use, and it always takes a comma in front of it · [clause], whereat [subject] [verb] — the reaction frame · the modern equivalents: on which, to which, with which, at which, upon which, and the stranded version at the end of the clause (the rock it stands on) · never ✗ with a human antecedent · never ✗ opening a sentence — every one of these points back at something already on the page
entries.contrast: Against by which, in which, on which: identical in meaning, opposite in register — the shelf on which it stood is ordinary formal English, the shelf whereon it stood is costume. Against the here- and there- families: all three are built the same way and used differently — where- relativizes and hooks a clause on, hereto and hereunder point at the document being signed, thereon and thereto point back at something already named, and it is the there- words, not these, that American lawyers still write every day (see thereon, thereto). Against wherefore: not a member of this set at all — it means "for which reason," and Juliet's wherefore art thou Romeo asks why, not where. Against the two-word where at of Where's he at?: that is the dialect question word and has nothing to do with this entry (see where at).
entries.variants: the rest of the family is built on the same pattern — wherein (= in which), whereby (= by which), whereof (= of which), and the rarer wherefrom and whereinto; the three that stand in for a noun phrase have their own entries at wherein, whereby, and whereof. Whereto and whereunto are the same word, unto being the older and heavier to. Wherewith survives in ordinary American English only as the noun it fathered, wherewithal — the wherewithal to pay.
entries.see also: by which, in which, on which, of which, which, the which, wherein, whereby, whereof, thereon, thereto, whereupon (conjunction), whereat (conjunction), whereon (conjunction), whereto (conjunction), wherewith (conjunction), whereunto (conjunction)
